about: The starter drill library for Clean Sheet.
Every entry here is written from scratch in our own words. Nothing is copied from
The FA's England Football Learning site, the FIFA Training Centre, or anywhere else.
Where a drill overlaps with a published FA or FIFA resource we link out to it as
further reading in `references` — we never reproduce their text, images or video.
See docs/content-policy.md before adding anything to this file.
References deliberately point at section landing pages rather than deep article
URLs, which rot quickly and would send coaches to a 404 mid-session.

drills.name: Traffic Lights
drills.summary: Ball-mastery warm-up where colours tell players to stop, go, or turn.
drills.description:
Every player has a ball inside the grid and dribbles freely. The coach calls a colour and the players react: **green** is dribble at speed into space, **amber** is slow it down with lots of small touches, **red** is stop the ball dead with the sole of the foot.

It gets a whole squad moving with a ball each inside thirty seconds, which is exactly what you want on a cold Tuesday when players are arriving in dribs and drabs. Add and remove players without stopping the activity.
drills.setup: A 20x20 yard grid marked with cones. One ball per player. Adjust the grid so it feels slightly crowded — players should have to lift their heads to avoid each other.
coachingPoints: Head up between touches — can you see the space before you move into it?
Use the sole of the foot to stop the ball cleanly on 'red'
Little touches when you're near someone, bigger touches when you're in space
Use both feet — try the next 'red' with your other foot
progressions: Add a colour for a turn (e.g. 'blue' = drag-back and go the other way)
Call two colours in a row so players have to hold a sequence in their head
Shrink the grid to increase the number of near-misses
regressions: Use just green and red until the group is confident
Make the grid bigger so there is less traffic to deal with

references.label: England Football Learning — coaching the youngest age groups

diagram.caption: Everyone has a ball; the coach calls a colour.

drills.name: Passing Gates
drills.summary: Pairs score a point every time they pass cleanly through any gate.
drills.description:
Scatter small cone gates around the area. In pairs with one ball, players move around and pass to each other through any gate they can find. A pass counts only if the ball goes through a gate and the partner controls it on the other side.

The scoring is what makes it work — pairs start hunting for gates rather than standing still, so you get movement, scanning and passing without ever telling anyone to move.
drills.setup: A 25x25 yard area with 8-10 gates made from pairs of cones, roughly 2 yards wide, scattered at all angles. One ball between two.
coachingPoints: Look for the gate before you receive, not after
Pass firmly — a soft pass through a gate is easy to intercept in a real game
Move to a new angle straight after you pass
Talk to your partner: tell them which gate you're heading for
progressions: Count as a pair and ask them to beat their own score in the next 90 seconds
No repeating the same gate twice in a row
Add two defenders who intercept and win the ball for their own count
regressions: Make the gates wider
Let the receiving player use as many touches as they need

references.label: England Football Learning — practice design and session planning

diagram.caption: Pairs score a point for every clean pass through any gate.

drills.name: Sharks and Minnows
drills.summary: Dribble across the area without losing your ball to the sharks.
drills.description:
The minnows line up on one side with a ball each. One or two sharks start in the middle with no ball. On the call, the minnows dribble to the far side. Sharks try to kick the balls out of the area.

A minnow who loses their ball becomes a shark, so the game gets harder as it goes and the last player standing has earned it. Everyone is involved the whole time — nobody is queuing.
drills.setup: A 20x25 yard area. One ball per minnow. Start with one shark for every eight players.
coachingPoints: Keep the ball close when a shark is near, push it further when the path is clear
Look up and pick the gap before you set off
Use your body between the shark and the ball
Change direction rather than running into trouble
progressions: Sharks must dribble the won ball out rather than just kicking it away
Narrow the area so there is less space to escape into
regressions: Widen the area
Sharks can only move sideways along the middle line
A player who loses the ball can retrieve it and rejoin as a minnow

diagram.caption: Minnows dribble across; sharks try to win the balls.

drills.name: Pass and Follow Triangle
drills.summary: Continuous passing round a triangle where you always follow your pass.
drills.description:
Three cones form a triangle with players split between them. Player passes to the next cone, then jogs to join the back of the queue they just passed to. The ball moves round the triangle continuously.

It looks simple, and it is — that is the point of a warm-up. What it does buy you is a lot of repetitions of a clean pass and a first touch out of the feet, plus a chance to see who is comfortable on their weaker side.
drills.setup: Three cones in a triangle roughly 8-10 yards apart. Two to four players at each cone. One ball per triangle; add a second ball once it is flowing.
coachingPoints: First touch out of your feet and into the direction you're passing
Pass along the ground with the inside of the foot
Call the name of the player you're passing to
Follow your pass at a jog, not a walk
progressions: Add a second ball going the other way round
Two touches maximum, then one
Receive with the back foot and open your body before passing
regressions: Shorten the distance between cones
Unlimited touches while players find their rhythm

diagram.caption: Pass, then follow your pass to the next cone.

drills.name: Ball Mastery Grid
drills.summary: Individual ball work: sole rolls, toe taps, drag-backs and turns.
drills.description:
Each player has a ball in their own small square. The coach demonstrates a move, players copy it for 45 seconds, then everyone dribbles to a new square before the next move.

Rotate through: sole rolls side to side, toe taps on top of the ball, drag-back turns, inside-outside touches, and the Cruyff turn. The moving-square bit matters — it keeps it feeling like a game rather than a drill, and it gets heads up between reps.
drills.setup: A grid of small 3x3 yard squares, one per player, marked with four cones each (or one cone if you're short). One ball per player.
coachingPoints: Quality over speed — get it right slowly first
Both feet, every time
Head up for a moment between each repetition
Stay on your toes, not flat-footed
progressions: Speed it up and count repetitions in 30 seconds
Players invent a move and teach it to the group
Perform the move then accelerate out of the square for three touches
regressions: Fewer moves, more time on each
Demonstrate alongside a player who has it, so there are two models to watch

references.label: FIFA Training Centre — grassroots coaching resources

diagram.caption: One small square each; move to a new one between moves.

drills.name: Rondo 4v1
drills.summary: Four players keep the ball in a square while one defender tries to win it.
drills.description:
Four attackers stand around the edges of a square, one defender inside. The attackers keep the ball away from the defender. If the defender wins it or forces it out, the player responsible goes in.

The rondo is the most efficient possession practice there is — high touches, constant decisions, and the defender never gets a rest. Keep the groups small so nobody is waiting.
drills.setup: A 10x10 yard square per group of five. Attackers stay on the edges; the defender works inside. One ball per square.
coachingPoints: Open your body before the ball arrives so you can see both ways out
Play the pass you can see, not the one you want to see
Move along your edge to open a passing line
Defender: close the nearest passing lane rather than chasing the ball
progressions: Two touches maximum, then one touch
Add a second defender to make it 4v2
A pass split between the two defenders counts double
regressions: Make the square bigger
Allow unlimited touches
Defender starts passive, only closing down at walking pace

references.label: England Football Learning — possession and playing out

diagram.caption: Four on the edges, one defender inside.

drills.name: Third-Man Runs in a Diamond
drills.summary: Practise the pass that sets up the pass — receiving from a player you didn't pass to.
drills.description:
Four players in a diamond. The player at the base passes to a side player, who sets it back or sideways, and the ball is then played on to the player at the top — who was moving before the ball came. The receiver at the top is the 'third man': they get the ball from a pass they were never part of.

This is one of the harder ideas to teach and one of the most valuable. Start slow and unopposed. The moment they see it work in a game it clicks.
drills.setup: A diamond of four cones roughly 10 yards apart. Four players per diamond, one ball. Rotate one position clockwise every two minutes.
coachingPoints: Third man: start your run before the second pass is played
Set the ball back with a firm, accurate touch — a bobbling set-back kills the move
Scan over your shoulder before you receive
Time the run so you arrive as the ball does, not before
progressions: Add a passive defender in the middle
Limit to two touches throughout
Finish the sequence with a shot or a pass into a target goal
regressions: Walk through the pattern with no ball first
Let the third man stand still and receive to feet

references.label: England Football Learning — attacking principles and combination play

diagram.caption: Base to side, set, then in behind to the third man.

drills.name: Two-Touch Passing Squares
drills.summary: Four players, one square, one ball — control and pass, endlessly.
drills.description:
Players stand on the four corners of a square. The ball goes round the square with two touches: one to control, one to pass. After ten clean circuits, change direction. After twenty, switch to diagonal passes across the square.

Unfussy and repetitive on purpose. Use it when the group needs to settle down and get some quality touches in before something more demanding.
drills.setup: A 12x12 yard square, one player per corner, one ball. Multiple squares run in parallel.
coachingPoints: First touch away from your body, into space
Second touch is the pass — no dawdling
Weight the pass so it arrives at a comfortable pace
Point at where you want the ball before it comes
progressions: One touch only
Follow your pass and swap corners
Add a second ball travelling the opposite way
regressions: Three touches allowed
Shrink the square so passes are shorter

diagram.caption: One touch to control, one to pass, round the square.

drills.name: First Touch Turn Gates
drills.summary: Receive with your back to the pitch, turn, and dribble through a gate.
drills.description:
A server plays a firm pass into a player standing with their back to the gates. The receiver takes one touch to turn out of the pass, then dribbles through any gate behind them. Then they become the server.

The skill being trained is the turn — the touch that takes you from facing the wrong way to facing the right way in a single movement. Encourage them to try different turns rather than always using the same one.
drills.setup: Servers on one line, receivers 8 yards away with their backs to three gates set 10 yards behind them. One ball per pair.
coachingPoints: Check over your shoulder before the ball arrives — which gate is free?
Open your hips as the ball comes so the first touch takes you round
Touch the ball into space, not under your feet
Accelerate away after the turn
progressions: Add a defender pressing from behind
Server calls the gate number as they pass
Two-touch limit: turn and go
regressions: Softer, slower service
Allow a controlling touch before the turning touch

diagram.caption: Receive with your back to the gates, turn, and go through one.

drills.name: 1v1 Gate Duels
drills.summary: Attacker tries to dribble through any of three gates; defender tries to stop them.
drills.description:
One attacker with a ball starts 10 yards from a defender. Behind the defender are three gates. The attacker scores by dribbling through any gate under control. The defender scores by winning the ball or forcing it out.

Three gates rather than one is the whole trick: the defender cannot simply stand in the way, so the attacker has to look up, pick a side, and commit. Swap roles every turn so everyone gets both jobs.
drills.setup: A 15x12 yard channel. Three gates spread across the end line, each 2 yards wide. Attackers queue at one end with a ball each.
coachingPoints: Attacker: run at the defender with the ball, not away from it — make them decide
Change of pace beats change of direction on its own
Defender: side-on stance, show them to one side, don't dive in
Defender: stay on your toes and close the space slowly
progressions: Reduce to two gates so decisions come faster
Defender starts closer, giving the attacker less time
Winner stays on and faces the next player
regressions: Widen the gates
Defender starts passive and only becomes live after the attacker's second touch

references.label: England Football Learning — 1v1 and individual possession

diagram.caption: Three gates to attack — the defender cannot cover them all.

drills.name: Beat the Defender Channels
drills.summary: Repeated 1v1s in narrow channels, so nobody hides and nobody queues.
drills.description:
Split the pitch into three or four narrow channels running end to end. Each channel has an attacker and a defender working continuously: attacker tries to reach the far line under control, then turns and goes back the other way against the same defender. Swap after 90 seconds.

The narrow channel forces a genuine 1v1 — there's nowhere to run around the problem. Short, sharp bursts with real rest in between.
drills.setup: Channels roughly 8 yards wide by 20 yards long, marked with cones. One ball per channel, two players per channel.
coachingPoints: Attacker: get the defender moving before you commit to a direction
Protect the ball with your body when the defender gets close
Defender: don't let them turn you — stay goal-side and patient
Defender: force them onto their weaker foot
progressions: Narrow the channel further
Add a time limit — 8 seconds to get to the far line
Winner of each duel moves up a channel, loser moves down
regressions: Widen the channel
Defender may only tackle inside the final five yards

diagram.caption: Narrow channels — nowhere to run around the problem.

drills.name: Shooting Ladder
drills.summary: Three shooting stations at increasing distance, run as a rotation.
drills.description:
Set three shooting positions: close range inside the box, edge of the box, and just outside. Players work round all three, one shot at each, then collect their ball and rejoin.

The point of the ladder is that the technique has to change with the distance — a side-foot finish close in, a firmer laces strike further out. Ask them what changed rather than telling them.
drills.setup: A goal with a keeper (or a target goal if you have none). Three cone positions at roughly 6, 14 and 20 yards. A supply of balls beside each position.
coachingPoints: Look at the goal before you look at the ball
Close range: side foot, accuracy over power, pick your corner
Longer range: laces, non-kicking foot alongside the ball, follow through
Head still and over the ball to keep the shot down
progressions: Add a pass in before the shot, so it's a moving ball
One-touch finishes only at the close station
Add a recovering defender chasing from behind
regressions: Move every station closer
Stationary ball, unlimited time

diagram.caption: Three stations — the technique changes with the distance.

drills.name: Cross and Finish Waves
drills.summary: Wide player delivers, two attackers arrive at the near and far post.
drills.description:
A wide player dribbles to the by-line and crosses. Two attackers start centrally and time their runs — one to the near post, one to the far. Alternate the side the cross comes from so both feet get used.

At younger ages the crossing itself is hard, so lower the expectation on the delivery and coach the runs. A cut-back along the ground counts as a cross and is often the better ball anyway.
drills.setup: Half a pitch with a goal and a keeper. Wide starting cones on both flanks, a queue of attackers in the centre circle. Plenty of balls with the wide players.
coachingPoints: Near-post runner: attack the ball, get in front of your defender
Far-post runner: stay wide and behind, arrive late
Crosser: head up before you deliver — where are they?
A cut-back along the ground is often better than a high cross
progressions: Add one or two defenders in the box
Add a third runner arriving at the edge of the area for the cut-back
First-time finishes only
regressions: Crosser can carry the ball to a set position and deliver unopposed with time
Attackers walk their runs through first with no ball

diagram.caption: Near-post and far-post runs, timed to the delivery.

drills.name: Press the Cone
drills.summary: Teach the approach: closing down under control rather than sprinting in.
drills.description:
A defender starts 10 yards from a cone with a ball on it. On the call they close the ball down, arriving side-on with short steps in the final two yards, and touch the ball with the sole of the foot without knocking the cone over.

Stripping out the attacker for a few minutes lets you actually coach the approach — which is the part most young defenders get wrong. Then put an attacker back in and see if it holds up.
drills.setup: Cones spread out with a ball resting beside each. Defenders in pairs, one working, one watching and giving feedback.
coachingPoints: Fast for the first two-thirds, slow for the last third
Arrive side-on, not square — show them one way
Small steps at the end so you can react either way
Stay on your toes with a low centre of gravity
progressions: Replace the cone with a live attacker who may go either way
Two defenders press together, one pressing and one covering
Add a time limit on the approach
regressions: Walk the approach through in slow motion
Shorten the starting distance

diagram.caption: Fast for two-thirds, slow and side-on for the last third.

drills.name: Goalkeeper Handling Circuit
drills.summary: Three stations of handling work — low, mid-height and diving.
drills.description:
Three short stations for your keeper (or keepers) to rotate through: rolled balls to gather low, waist-height balls into a secure chest catch, and balls thrown wide to dive and hold.

Most grassroots keepers get no specific work at all, so ten focused minutes goes a long way. If you only have one keeper, pair them with an outfield player who fancies a go — it usually reveals someone.
drills.setup: One goal or a marked 5-yard area. A server with a supply of balls at each station. Cones marking the working area.
coachingPoints: Hands behind the ball, fingers spread, thumbs together for high balls
Get your body behind the line of the ball wherever possible
Low balls: get down early, don't reach with hands alone
Hold it if you can, push it wide of the post if you can't
progressions: Serve without announcing the height
Add a shot from a moving ball
Keeper distributes accurately to a target after each save
regressions: Slow underarm serves, straight at the keeper
Kneeling starts for the diving station so there is less to think about

diagram.caption: Low, mid-height, then diving — rotate through.

drills.name: Y-Drill Combination
drills.summary: Pass, set, spin — a repeatable three-player combination ending in a shot.
drills.description:
A midfielder passes into a striker who has come short. The striker sets it first-time to a supporting player, who plays it into the path of the midfielder spinning off into the space behind. Finish with a shot.

Unopposed to begin with, so the pattern lands. It is the same idea as the third-man run but with a goal at the end, which tends to hold attention better.
drills.setup: A Y shape of cones on the edge of the final third, with a goal. Three players per repetition, plus a keeper. Rotate positions after each go.
coachingPoints: Striker: come towards the ball, don't wait for it
The set-back must be first time and firm
Spin off the shoulder as the set is played, not before
Take the shot early — the space closes fast
progressions: Add a defender marking the striker
One touch throughout the combination
Alternate sides so both feet are used
regressions: Walk the pattern with no defenders and no time pressure
Allow two touches on the set-back

diagram.caption: Pass in, set back, spin off into the space behind.

drills.name: 4v4 Four-Goal Game
drills.summary: Two teams, four mini goals — attack whichever one is unguarded.
drills.description:
Two teams of four play in a square with two small goals to attack on opposite sides. Because there are two goals to defend, teams get pulled apart and space appears constantly.

This is the small-sided game we come back to most. Everyone touches the ball, the picture changes every few seconds, and switching play stops being an abstract instruction and becomes the obvious thing to do.
drills.setup: A 30x25 yard area. Two mini goals (or cone goals) on each end line, set wide apart. Bibs for one team. One ball, with spares around the edge to keep it flowing.
coachingPoints: Which goal is less protected? Attack that one
Switch the ball quickly when one side gets crowded
Spread out when you have the ball, squeeze together when you don't
First defender presses, everyone else slides across
progressions: Must score in a different goal from the last one
Three-touch maximum
Add a neutral player who always plays for the team in possession
regressions: Bigger area, fewer players
Widen the goals
Remove touch limits entirely

references.label: England Football Learning — small-sided games and youth formats
FIFA Training Centre — grassroots small-sided football

diagram.caption: Two goals each to attack — the pitch keeps stretching.

drills.name: 3v3 End Zone Game
drills.summary: Score by dribbling or passing into the end zone and controlling the ball there.
drills.description:
Two teams of three. Instead of goals, each team attacks an end zone: a point is scored when a player controls the ball inside the opposition zone, having received it there or dribbled in.

Taking the goals away shifts the focus onto getting the ball forward and supporting the player who has it. It also means no keeper, so all six players are in the game.
drills.setup: A 25x20 yard area with 3-yard end zones marked at each end. Bibs for one team. One ball.
coachingPoints: Support in front of and behind the ball, not alongside
Can you play forward? If not, keep it and wait
Time your run into the end zone — don't camp in it
Defenders: protect the zone first, press the ball second
progressions: Ball must be passed into the zone, not dribbled
Two-touch limit
Play 3v3 plus a floating neutral
regressions: Deeper end zones
Larger area
Allow a player to stand permanently in the end zone as a target

diagram.caption: Control the ball in the end zone to score.

drills.name: 2v2 Continuous Duels
drills.summary: Rolling 2v2s to goal — win it, attack it, and the next pair comes straight on.
drills.description:
Two attackers take on two defenders towards a goal with a keeper. As soon as the ball goes dead, the coach serves a new ball to the next waiting pair from the opposite side, and the previous defenders become the new attackers.

Continuous means nobody stands still and the transition moment — the second the ball changes hands — happens over and over, which is exactly the moment most goals come from.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, one goal with a keeper. Two queues of pairs on either side of the halfway line. A big supply of balls with the coach.
coachingPoints: Attackers: one goes, one supports — never both in the same space
Attack the goal quickly before the defenders are set
Defenders: one presses, one covers behind
React the instant the ball turns over — first two seconds decide it
progressions: Serve to the defenders sometimes, so they must counter-attack
10-second time limit to score
Make it 3v2 to create an overload
regressions: Longer gaps between serves so players can reset
Play 2v1 in the attackers' favour

diagram.caption: Ball goes dead, next pair comes straight on.

drills.name: Overload 4v2 to Goal
drills.summary: Four attackers against two defenders — use the extra players properly.
drills.description:
Four attackers try to score against two defenders and a keeper. If the defenders win the ball, they score by dribbling over the halfway line.

The overload is deliberate: with a two-player advantage there is almost always a free player, and the coaching is about finding them rather than forcing it. Give the defenders a real way to score or they stop trying.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, goal and keeper at one end, halfway line as the defenders' target. Bibs for the defenders. Rotate roles every three minutes.
coachingPoints: Find the free player — there is always one
Move the defenders with the ball before you commit
Width first, then attack the space it creates
Defenders: stay compact and delay; don't both go to the ball
progressions: Reduce to 4v3
Two-touch limit for the attackers
Attackers must score within 15 seconds
regressions: Make it 5v2
Defenders start passive for the first three passes

diagram.caption: Two spare players — the coaching is finding them.

drills.name: 5v5 Two-Touch Game
drills.summary: A normal small-sided game with a two-touch limit to speed up the thinking.
drills.description:
A standard 5v5 with goals and keepers, but nobody may take more than two touches. The restriction forces players to decide where the ball is going before it arrives.

Use it as a follow-on once a passing theme has been introduced. Expect it to be scrappy for the first three minutes — let them work through that rather than stopping it.
drills.setup: A 40x30 yard pitch with a goal at each end. Bibs for one team. Spare balls behind each goal.
coachingPoints: Decide before the ball arrives — scan early and often
First touch sets up the second, so make it count
Off the ball: give them an easy option, quickly
Angles, not straight lines — make yourself passable to
progressions: One touch only for two minutes
A goal scored first-time counts double
regressions: Three touches
Remove the limit in your own half only
Bigger pitch to buy more time

diagram.caption: Two touches maximum — decide before it arrives.

drills.name: Score in Any Goal
drills.summary: Four goals scattered around the area, both teams can score in any of them.
drills.description:
Set four mini goals at random points inside the playing area rather than on the lines. Both teams may score in any goal, from either side. Defenders have to think about four targets at once, so they can never be fully organised.

Chaotic in the best way. Brilliant for younger groups and for the end of a session when concentration is fading but energy isn't.
drills.setup: A 30x30 yard area with four mini goals (or cone goals) placed inside it, well away from the edges. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Head up — which goal has nobody near it?
Change direction quickly when a goal gets covered
Look for the goal behind the defence, not just in front of you
Defend the ball and the nearest goal at the same time
progressions: Must use a different goal each time
Only score with a first-time finish
regressions: Fewer players in the same area
Widen the goals

diagram.caption: Four goals inside the area — look for the empty one.

drills.name: Playing Out From the Back 6v4
drills.summary: Build from the keeper against a pressing forward line and beat the first press.
drills.description:
A keeper plus a back four and a midfielder try to play out of their own third against four pressing attackers. The defending team succeeds by getting the ball under control past a line of cones at the halfway point. The attackers score in the goal if they win it.

The realistic bit is the pressure — if the attackers aren't genuinely trying, nobody learns anything. Give them a real incentive to win it back.
drills.setup: One third of a pitch, a full goal and keeper at one end, a line of cones marking the target line. Bibs for the pressing team.
coachingPoints: Get wide and deep early to stretch the press
The keeper is a player — use them to switch the ball
Play through the press when you can, over it when you can't
If the first option isn't on, go back and around — don't force it
progressions: Add a fifth presser
Two-touch limit for the defending team
Attackers must press within three seconds of the ball being played
regressions: Fewer pressers, making it 6v3
Pressers may not enter the penalty area
Walk it through unopposed once first

references.label: England Football Learning — playing out from the back

diagram.caption: Beat the press and get the ball over the line under control.

drills.name: Defending the Middle Third
drills.summary: A back four and two midfielders defend as a unit against an attacking six.
drills.description:
Six attackers try to get through the middle third and score. Six defenders work as a unit to stop them, scoring themselves by winning it and playing into either of two wide target zones.

The focus is the shape between the players rather than the individual tackle. Freeze it occasionally and ask the defenders where they'd be if the ball were five yards further left.
drills.setup: The middle third of a pitch plus a goal at one end. Two wide target zones behind the defending team's starting position. Bibs for one team.
coachingPoints: Press the ball, everyone else shifts across together
Stay compact — no gaps between the lines for them to play into
Show them wide, away from the middle
Communicate: someone tells the unit when to step up
progressions: Give the attackers a time limit to break through
Add a seventh attacker to create an overload
Defenders must make three passes after winning it
regressions: Reduce the attackers to five
Narrow the playing area
Walk the shifting shape through slowly with the ball being moved by hand

references.label: England Football Learning — defending as a team

diagram.caption: Press the ball, everyone else shifts across together.

drills.name: Attacking Wide Areas 7v5
drills.summary: Attack with an overload and use the width to create a chance.
drills.description:
Seven attackers play against five defenders and a keeper in the attacking half. Wide channels are marked, and a goal scored from a cross or cut-back originating in a channel counts double.

The double-points rule does the coaching for you — players start looking for the wide player without being told. Rotate the defending group often; it's hard work.
drills.setup: Half a pitch, one goal with a keeper. Wide channels 6 yards deep marked down both flanks. Bibs for the defenders.
coachingPoints: Get the ball wide early, before the defence is set
Someone must attack the near post every single time
Cut-backs beat high crosses more often than you'd think
Overlap or underlap — give the wide player a decision to make
progressions: Reduce to 6v5
Limit the attack to 20 seconds
Defenders counter into a target goal on halfway
regressions: Only one defender allowed in each wide channel
Make it 8v4

diagram.caption: A goal from a wide delivery counts double.

drills.name: Conditioned Match: Three Passes
drills.summary: A normal match, but a team must string three passes together before scoring.
drills.description:
Play a regular match with one condition: three consecutive passes by the attacking team before a goal counts. It rewards the group that keeps the ball rather than the one that hoofs it and chases.

Drop the condition for the last five minutes and just let them play. That final stretch of free football is the bit most of them came for, and it's worth protecting.
drills.setup: The largest pitch and biggest goals you have. Even teams, bibs for one side. Spare balls all round the outside so restarts are quick.
coachingPoints: Count the passes out loud as a team
Keep the pitch big when you have it, small when you don't
Look forward first — the condition isn't an excuse to go sideways
Support the player on the ball quickly
progressions: Increase to five passes
Passes must include a switch from one side to the other
regressions: Two passes
Remove the condition and play freely

diagram.caption: Three consecutive passes before a goal counts.

drills.name: Free Play Match
drills.summary: Let them play. Coach with questions, not instructions.
drills.description:
A straight match with no conditions. The coach stays quiet for long stretches and, when the ball goes out, asks a question rather than giving an answer: *what did you see there?*, *what else could you have done?*, *what would you try next time?*

This is the hardest thing on the list to do well, because the instinct is to shout. Resist it. The players' own answers stick far better than anything shouted from the touchline.
drills.setup: The biggest pitch you can mark out, proper goals if you have them. Even teams. Bibs. Spare balls around the edges.
coachingPoints: Ask, don't tell — one question per stoppage at most
Let mistakes play out; the game is the teacher
Praise the attempt, not just the outcome
Rotate positions so nobody gets stuck in one role every week
progressions: Rotate positions every five minutes
Give each player one individual challenge to work on
regressions: Smaller pitch and fewer players so everyone gets more touches
Play in two separate smaller games rather than one big one

references.label: FIFA Training Centre — grassroots coaching philosophy

drills.name: Cool-Down Circle
drills.summary: Gentle movement, then two questions that make the session stick.
drills.description:
Bring everyone into a circle. Two minutes of easy movement and stretching while you talk, then ask two questions: *what's one thing you did well tonight?* and *what's one thing you'll try next week?*

Going round the circle means every player says something out loud, including the quiet ones. It takes three minutes and it is the part players most often repeat to their parents in the car.
drills.setup: A circle in the middle of the pitch. No equipment needed. Balls collected and bagged first so nobody is fiddling with one.
coachingPoints: Every player speaks — go round the circle, don't take volunteers
Accept every answer without correcting it
Name one specific thing you saw from each player if you can
Finish on time; parents are waiting and it builds trust
progressions: Players nominate a teammate for something they did well
Set an individual challenge for the week ahead
regressions: One question instead of two
Thumbs up or down instead of speaking, for shy groups

references.label: England Football Learning — reflection and player development

diagram.caption: Everyone speaks — go round the circle rather than taking hands up.

drills.name: Juggling Challenge Cool-Down
drills.summary: Low-intensity individual and partner juggling to wind down.
drills.description:
Each player takes a ball and sees how many touches they can keep going. Then in pairs, working together to keep one ball up between them.

Calm, individual, and genuinely good for touch. It also gives you a couple of minutes to have a quiet word with one or two players without stopping the whole group.
drills.setup: Anywhere with space. One ball per player, then one between two.
coachingPoints: Small, soft touches — don't kick it, cushion it
Laces or thigh, keep the ankle locked
Beat your own score, not anyone else's
In pairs, tell your partner before you play it to them
progressions: Alternate feet on every touch
Add a knee or head touch into the sequence
In pairs, one touch each before it goes back
regressions: Allow a bounce between touches
Catch after every two touches, then restart
